plain_english: The wise person's raw material is their own mind. The doctor works with bodies. The person who gives massages works with bodies too. The farmer works with land. The wise person's job is to handle their impressions correctly — the way nature intended. Every soul naturally agrees with truth and disagrees with lies. When something is unclear, the soul stays uncertain. The soul naturally wants good things and avoids bad things. When something is neither good nor bad, the soul doesn't care either way. Think of a banker — he can't refuse Caesar's money. Neither can someone selling vegetables. If you show them the coin, they have to accept it and give you what you're buying, whether they want to or not. The soul works the same way. When something truly good appears, it immediately attracts the soul. Evil repels it. The soul will never reject something that's clearly good, just like people won't reject Caesar's coin. This principle drives everything both humans and gods do.
original_excerpt: The material for the wise and good man is his own ruling faculty: and the body is the material for the physician and the aliptes (the man who oils persons); the land is the matter for the husbandman. The business of the wise and good man is to use appearances conformably to nature: and as it is the nature of every soul to assent to the truth, to dissent from the false, and to remain in suspense as to that which is uncertain; so it is its nature to be moved towards the desire for the good, and to aversion from the evil; and with respect to that which is neither good nor bad it feels indifferent. For as the money-changer (banker) is not allowed to reject Cæsar's coin, nor the seller of herbs, but if you show the coin, whether he chooses or not, he must give up what is sold for the coin; so it is also in the matter of the soul. When the good appears, it immediately attracts to itself; the evil repels from itself. But the soul will never reject the manifest appearance of the good, any more than persons will reject Cæsar's coin. On this principle depends every movement both of man and God.
source_reference: Discourses, What is the Matter on Which a Good Man Should Be Employed, and in What We Ought Chiefly to Practise Ourselves

plain_english: This is the main thing you should practice. The moment you step outside in the morning, look at everyone you see and hear. Ask yourself: What did I just see? A good-looking man or woman? Use the rule. Is this up to you or not? It's not up to you. Dismiss it. What did you see? Someone crying over their dead child? Use the rule. Death is not up to you. Dismiss it. Did you run into a government official? Use the rule. What is a government position? Is it up to you or not? It's not up to you. Dismiss this too. It doesn't pass the test. Throw it out. It's nothing to you.
original_excerpt: Against (or with respect to) this kind of thing chiefly a man should exercise himself. As soon as you go out in the morning, examine every man whom you see, every man whom you hear; answer as to a question, What have you seen? A handsome man or woman? Apply the rule. Is this independent of the will, or dependent? Independent. Take it away. What have you seen? A man lamenting over the death of a child. Apply the rule. Death is a thing independent of the will. Take it away. Has the proconsul met you? Apply the rule. What kind of a thing is a proconsul's office? Independent of the will or dependent on it? Independent. Take this away also; it does not stand examination; cast it away; it is nothing to you.
source_reference: Discourses, What is the Matter on Which a Good Man Should Be Employed, and in What We Ought Chiefly to Practise Ourselves

plain_english: If we practiced this and worked on it every day from morning to night, we'd actually get somewhere. But instead, we get caught off guard by every impression that comes our way. We're half asleep most of the time. Maybe — just maybe — we wake up a little when we're in class. Then we go outside. We see someone crying and think, "He's ruined." We see a government official and think, "He's got it made." We see someone in exile and think, "He's miserable." We see a poor person and think, "He's suffering — he has nothing to eat."
original_excerpt: If we practised this and exercised ourselves in it daily from morning to night, something indeed would be done. But now we are forthwith caught half asleep by every appearance, and it is only, if ever, that in the school we are roused a little. Then when we go out, if we see a man lamenting, we say, He is undone. If we see a consul, we say, He is happy. If we see an exiled man, we say, He is miserable. If we see a poor man, we say, He is wretched; he has nothing to eat.
source_reference: Discourses, What is the Matter on Which a Good Man Should Be Employed, and in What We Ought Chiefly to Practise Ourselves

plain_english: We need to get rid of these bad opinions. That's where all our effort should go. What is crying and complaining? Just opinion. What is bad luck? Opinion. What are riots, arguments, blame, accusations, disrespect, or petty concerns? All of these are just opinions — nothing more. They're opinions about things outside your control, as if those things were good or bad. Let someone shift these opinions to things within their control, and I promise you they'll stay steady no matter what happens around them. Think of a bowl of water with light shining on it. Your soul is like that water. The things that happen to you are like the light ray hitting the water. When you shake the water, the light ray looks like it's moving too, but it's not really moving. When someone gets dizzy and confused, their skills and character don't actually get scrambled — it's just the mind they're written on that gets shaken up. Once the mind settles down, everything else settles back into place too.
original_excerpt: We ought then to eradicate these bad opinions, and to this end we should direct all our efforts. For what is weeping and lamenting? Opinion. What is bad fortune? Opinion. What is civil sedition, what is divided opinion, what is blame, what is accusation, what is impiety, what is trifling? All these things are opinions, and nothing more, and opinions about things independent of the will, as if they were good and bad. Let a man transfer these opinions to things dependent on the will, and I engage for him that he will be firm and constant, whatever may be the state of things around him. Such as is a dish of water, such is the soul. Such as is the ray of light which falls on the water, such are the appearances. When the water is moved, the ray also seems to be moved, yet it is not moved. And when then a man is seized with giddiness, it is not the arts and the virtues which are confounded, but the spirit (the nervous power) on which they are impressed; but if the spirit be restored to its settled state, those things also are restored.
source_reference: Discourses, What is the Matter on Which a Good Man Should Be Employed, and in What We Ought Chiefly to Practise Ourselves
